metadata.designIntent: Teach preview UI. Seed the perceived/actual trust gap on turn 1: promises inflate perception more than reality. `flag_ambitious_public_image` is referenced by Act II media cards ("Whatever happened to the big change?"). REPLAY: Act 0 is no longer a fixed chain — this card opens, the four pledge scenes arrive in seeded order from the entry pool, two seed-chosen 'first days' scenes fill act-turns 2 and 4, and the dinner invitation closes at act-turn 7.

Responsible action = more work, delayed payoff. The scheduled event lands early in Act I (card 010). Right is not punished — silence is the realistic default and its cost is invisible. REPLAY: now drawn from the entry pool as early as act-turn 1, so the follow-up waits (retry_later) until Act I has begun rather than landing inside the opening.
Both options are crowd-pleasers; the right one is *more* popular and grants Power — punishment politics pays better than procedure politics. First precedent of the run, invisible.
First alignment fork: public principle vs. establishment signal. Neither is corrupt. The Right answer is what every real politician says — and it is genuinely how things pass.
The Mentor's thesis is the game's thesis, inverted: he is *right* that relationships pass reforms. The game never argues with him. It just remembers.

End of Act 0. Attending creates no obligation — deliberately. The room costs nothing to enter. That is the point of the room. REPLAY: the envelope reads differently to the player who told the Mentor independence mattered more, and to the one who told the press reform requires cooperation.

Chain A root. The first real obligation of the run, priced generously: +6 Standing for one word. Refusing costs nothing visible — only the Mentor's warmth. REPLAY: the Mentor frames the seat through the player's first speech — the big-change promise, or the modest one.
Chain C root. No request, no obligation, no money. The corrupt network's first move is always free.

The declined network keeps functioning without the player. The permit still went through — someone else made the call. Both choices are deliberately empty: watching costs nothing and changes nothing, which is exactly the sentence this card is writing. Refusal removes you from the machine; it does not stop the machine. No relationship, no flag, no follow-up — he never looks the player's way again for the rest of the run.

Chain C link 2. **Deliberately no obligation and no money** — after this favor, *he* owes *you*. Gratitude is the hook: it converts into "access" (card 022, protected investment) which is where the real capture happens. The player should feel generous here, not bribed.

The pack's cleanest actual/perceived split. Publishing: elites recoil (Standing −), the real public quietly banks it (Actual ++, but Perceived lags — no one polls gratitude). Quiet resolution genuinely helps the family too — the promoted official is simply never named. Both defensible. That's the trap working as intended.
Chain B root. The line "I choose the questions" is the entire media-capture arc in six words; the player will re-read it very differently at card 049.

Chain D root. The only Act I card where the "good" option visibly costs two stats at once. `flag_public_reform_support` gates cards 031/038/052 and ultimately the Ending G payoff line: "Your office has no authority over this inquiry."
The nephew is *genuinely qualified* — stated twice. Nepotism's first step never requires hiring anyone unqualified. The precedent is what matters, and precedents don't check CVs.

**The most important card in Act I.** Bypassing procedure produces real, unambiguous good — dry homes, grateful residents, deserved trust. The mechanism that drains a flooded district is the same mechanism that will later bury an investigation. The game must never say this. The precedent counter says it.

The mechanical thesis in miniature: free refusal has already quietly expired if you took card 007. And the sting — the *only way to clear* the Mentor's debt is to do the thing he wants: you repay an obligation by acquiring a precedent. The ledger balances; the player doesn't. First cost-lock must land before turn ~10 so the Milestone-3 experience ("choice → advantage → obligation → later resistance") is proven inside Act I.

A palate-cleanser that still teaches the perception economy: claiming credit *works*, and Perceived Trust is the stat advisors will quote back later. `flag_self_promotional_style` modulates Act II media card wording.

The cheapest obligation in the game — weight 1, attached to a dinner. Teaches that obligations attach to *comfort*, not just contracts. Also the run's first meaningful money interaction: paying your own way should feel slightly, memorably annoying ($600 against $50,000 — the pain is symbolic and that's the lesson).

First divergence where "fixing" trust *lowers* actual trust: managed coverage reads as managed. The aide's "wrong on the details — mostly" is written to sting precisely when the rumor is half-true (player took 007 right) while remaining innocuous otherwise — one line, two readings, zero conditional text.
The loyalty machine pays out immediately and asks nothing. Both choices set the world-state flag (the secretary exists either way); only Left *uses* him — a small distinction the Aftermath remembers.

Independence rendered as friction, not catastrophe: your items just… wait. The machine doesn't punish; it deprioritizes. Neither choice fixes it — the point is that the vote you didn't cast still governs your Thursday.

The single permitted moment of near-commentary in Act I, delivered as a character's opinion, conditional on the player having actually earned it, and mechanically toothless — no stat punishes ignoring her. If the player's precedent counters are all zero, this card never appears: clean runs get no sermon.

Act I closes on the run's largest stat jump, sourced ambiguously on purpose ("the unofficial version depends on who is telling it"). The variant obligation is weight 2 — the heaviest debt so far — attached to the most flattering moment so far. Declining is rare but must stay viable (Standing −3, not a death sentence) and is remembered by Act II wording. REPLAY: the unofficial version of the promotion is spelled out by state — two other names in it, or for once the same story as the letter.

ACT 0 slot A (seed bucket 0/3): first-day logistics. Keeping the predecessor's machine is faster and buys the room's goodwill; bringing your own people costs a week and earns the Aide. Both small, both remembered.
ACT 0 slot A (seed bucket 1/3): procedure vs compassion in miniature. Seeing them now costs the party breakfast; scheduling them properly is what everyone else does. Neither is corrupt.
ACT 0 slot A (seed bucket 2/3): the first photograph decides which room you belong to. The atrium with the Mentor is the establishment signal; the constituency office is the other one.

ACT 0 slot B (seed bucket 0/2): the binder nobody reads. Reading it is a small, private form of power; the summary is what the Aide wrote for you, and reading only that is the first delegation of your judgment.
ACT 0 slot B (seed bucket 1/2): the predecessor offers 'context'. Taking the call inherits a map of the room and, quietly, its assumptions; declining keeps your view your own and costs you the map.
